title: Ultra-Processed Foods Are Now Linked to a Doubled Risk of Oesophageal Cancer — and the Threat May Be Greater for Diaspora Indians
excerpt: A new multi-cancer study finds that high UPF intake raises oesophageal cancer risk by 129% and stomach cancer by 56%, adding to evidence that should alarm anyone who has swapped home-cooked dal for packaged meals
body:
The evidence against ultra-processed foods has been building for years. But a new study published in *Frontiers in Nutrition* sharpens the warning into something harder to ignore: eating the most ultra-processed food more than doubles the risk of oesophageal cancer and raises stomach cancer risk by more than half.

The PANESOES study, conducted across a Mediterranean region of Spain, analysed 1,218 participants — including 193 oesophageal cancer cases, 412 stomach cancer cases, 161 pancreatic cancer cases, and 452 healthy controls. Researchers assessed what participants ate over a five-year window using a validated food frequency questionnaire, classifying foods by the NOVA system, the global standard for measuring processing levels.

The results were stark. People in the highest third of ultra-processed food consumption faced a 129% greater risk of oesophageal cancer (RRR 2.29, 95% CI: 1.37–3.82) and a 56% greater risk of stomach cancer (RRR 1.56, 95% CI: 1.08–2.27) compared to those who ate the least. Specific categories drove the risk further: ultra-processed dairy products doubled stomach cancer risk (RRR 2.10), while sweets and pastries raised it by 76%. Ultra-processed drinks and pre-cooked convenience foods were linked to higher oesophageal cancer risk.

No significant association was found with pancreatic cancer — but the gastrointestinal findings alone were enough to prompt the authors to call for further investigation and dietary policy action.

A Growing Body of Evidence

The PANESOES study does not stand alone. A comprehensive review published this year in *Cancer Epidemiology, Biomarkers & Prevention* synthesised the evidence across colorectal, gastric, oesophageal, and pancreatic cancers. It found that the strongest and most consistent link is with colorectal cancer, where the highest UPF consumers face a 10–30% increased risk. But the gastric and oesophageal evidence is catching up fast.

> "It found that the strongest and most consistent link is with colorectal cancer, where the highest UPF consumers face a 10–30% increased risk."

The mechanisms are increasingly well understood. Ultra-processing disrupts the natural food matrix, accelerating glycaemic absorption and activating insulin-like growth factor signalling — a known cancer pathway. Low fibre content and chemical additives alter the gut microbiome, reduce short-chain fatty acid production, impair intestinal barrier integrity, and promote chronic low-grade inflammation. Nitrates, nitrites, and emulsifiers found in processed meats, ready meals, and packaged snacks have demonstrated pro-inflammatory and carcinogenic effects in laboratory studies.

A separate 2026 paper in *NPJ Metabolic Health and Disease* reinforced that UPF-rich diets independently increase energy intake and weight gain through hyper-palatable formulations and faster eating rates — effects that compound the cancer risk through obesity pathways.

Why This Matters More for Diaspora Indians

For the estimated 32 million Indians living abroad, particularly in the US, UK, and Canada, the dietary transition from traditional cooking to Western convenience food is not a lifestyle footnote — it is a health inflection point.

India’s traditional food culture — built around freshly prepared lentils, vegetables, whole grains, and spices — is inherently low in ultra-processed ingredients. Turmeric, cumin, and ginger carry documented anti-inflammatory properties. Home-cooked rotis, sabzis, and dals are about as far from the NOVA Group 4 classification as food can get.

But diaspora life, with its dual-income households, long commutes, and children raised on Western school lunches, often pushes families toward exactly the foods this research indicts: packaged cereals, frozen meals, processed cheese, sugary drinks, instant noodles, and pre-made sauces. Studies from the US and UK consistently show that ultra-processed foods now account for 55–60% of total caloric intake in high-income Western countries.

South Asians already carry a disproportionate burden of metabolic disease — higher rates of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and visceral fat accumulation at lower BMI thresholds. Adding elevated gastrointestinal cancer risk from dietary westernisation makes the picture significantly worse.

What Can Actually Be Done

The research does not suggest that every packaged item is a carcinogen. The NOVA classification distinguishes between minimally processed foods (frozen vegetables, plain yoghurt), processed foods (canned beans, cheese), and ultra-processed products (soft drinks, instant noodles, packaged snacks with long ingredient lists). The risk concentrates in Group 4 — products with ingredients you would not find in a home kitchen.

Practical steps are straightforward, if not always easy:

  • **Batch cooking on weekends** — preparing dal, rice, curries, and rotis in advance — can dramatically reduce weekday reliance on packaged convenience food.
  • **Reading ingredient lists** — if it contains emulsifiers, artificial flavourings, or ingredients you cannot pronounce, it is likely ultra-processed.
  • **Swapping drinks** — replacing sweetened beverages with water, buttermilk, or unsweetened chai eliminates one of the highest-risk categories identified in the study.
  • **Choosing whole snacks** — roasted makhana, fresh fruit, or homemade chivda over packaged chips and biscuits.

The PANESOES study is observational, not a randomised trial, and the authors are careful to note that further research is needed. But the direction of evidence — across multiple cancers, multiple countries, and multiple research teams — is now unmistakable. Ultra-processed food is not just making people heavier. It may be making them sicker in ways that take years to surface.

For a diaspora community already navigating elevated metabolic risk, that is a warning worth acting on before the diagnosis arrives.
